analysis.one_liner: Bars colleges from using federal student aid for programs that leave graduates unqualified for the licenses they were advertised to prepare for.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in the final month of the 117th Congress, never received a hearing or vote, and expired with zero cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would cut colleges off from federal student aid — including Pell Grants, federal loans, workforce funding, and GI Bill and other military education benefits — if their degree or certificate programs do not actually qualify graduates to take the licensing exams in the occupations they advertise for. It also requires schools to arrange required clinical placements and internships, certify each career-focused program's accreditation and licensure prerequisites to the Education Department, get a signed warning from any student enrolling in a program that fails those prerequisites, and be legally authorized in every state where its online students live.
analysis.who_benefits: Students — especially working adults, career-changers, and military veterans — who enroll in programs leading to licensed occupations like nursing, trucking, or cosmetology. The bill targets a known problem: schools that collect federal aid for programs whose graduates cannot legally work in the field they paid to enter. Students in those states and online programs get advance written warning before enrolling in a program that will not make them licensable where they live.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Students in licensed-occupation programs, including veterans

how_it_helps.text: A college loses federal student aid eligibility for any program meant to prepare students for a licensed occupation unless completing it fully qualifies the student to take the required licensing exam and meet state licensing prerequisites — including in every state the school advertises to — and the school provides timely clinical placements, internships, or apprenticeships.

Schools must certify to the Education Department that each career-focused (gainful employment) program is approved by a recognized accreditor, meets applicable programmatic accreditation, and satisfies educational prerequisites for licensure; a program found ineligible cannot be re-established for at least three years.

If a program does not satisfy licensure prerequisites in a student's intended state, the school must notify the student and obtain a signed, handwritten acknowledgement that the student still wants to enroll — so students know what they are getting before spending aid money.

The protections cover not just Title IV (Pell Grants and federal loans) but also workforce funding, adult education funding, veterans' education benefits under title 38, and military tuition programs under title 10 — closing the doors through which problematic programs previously re-entered.

Online and correspondence programs must be legally authorized in every state where their enrolled students live, subject to state authorization reciprocity agreements with complaint-handling requirements.

analysis.who_pays: Colleges and universities running licensure-track career programs — most directly for-profit career colleges and online schools — face new certification, accreditation, placement, and state-authorization requirements, and lose access to federal aid entirely for programs that fail the licensure test. The Education Department takes on certification and oversight work.
analysis.who_pays_short: For-profit career colleges and online programs

drawbacks.text: The bill requires schools to provide timely placement for clinical placements, internships, and apprenticeships, but those slots are controlled by outside employers and hospitals; a school could lose all federal aid eligibility because a third party has no openings.

The enforcement for students already in a non-qualifying program is only a written warning: a school may still enroll a student in a program that fails licensure prerequisites as long as the student signs a handwritten acknowledgement wishing to enroll anyway — meaning some students still graduate with a credential they cannot use.

Legitimate schools, including community colleges and traditional universities, must document licensure prerequisites in every state they advertise to and in every state where online students reside, a compliance burden that could lead some to restrict which states' students they accept.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core idea — federal aid should not fund degrees that leave students unemployable in the licensed fields they trained for — addresses a real and documented harm with serious stakes for students. The design is uneven: the third-party placement requirement may punish schools for failures they cannot control, and the signed-warning provision tolerates continued enrollment in non-qualifying programs. Still, the bill's cost falls mainly on schools, while the protection falls to students who borrow or use GI benefits to pay for these programs.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in the last month of the 117th Congress and referred to three House committees, and none of them acted before the Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

narrative.text: Rep. Raja Krishnamoorthi introduced the bill on December 6, 2022, in the final month of the 117th Congress.
The same day, it was referred to the House Education and Labor Committee and, in addition, to the Armed Services and Veterans' Affairs Committees.
The action history shows no hearings, markups, committee votes, or floor action of any kind after the referral, and the Congress ended on January 3, 2023.
No other member cosponsored the bill; the cosponsor list was empty.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Schools running licensure-track programs that would have faced aid cutoffs, certification requirements, and placement obligations keep the status quo: they can continue enrolling students into programs that may not lead to licensure, using federal aid, GI Bill benefits, and federal workforce funding. Students in those programs gained nothing.

for.name: Rep. Raja Krishnamoorthi
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and served as its sole sponsor.

against.name: House Education and Labor Committee
against.role: Committee of primary jurisdiction; no action taken
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on December 6, 2022, and took no further action — no hearing, markup, or vote — before the Congress ended.

against.name: House Armed Services Committee and House Veterans' Affairs Committee
against.role: Additional committees of referral; no action taken
against.what_they_did: Received the referral for portions of the bill touching military and veterans' education benefits and took no recorded action before the Congress ended.

against.name: House colleagues of both parties
against.what_they_did: Not one member of the House joined as a cosponsor in the bill's four weeks of existence.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken and no member cosponsored, so the record shows only a single Democratic sponsor and no measurable support or opposition from either party.

industries.note: These schools sell licensure-track programs to students paying with federal aid and GI benefits; the bill would cut off federal funding for any program whose graduates cannot qualify for the advertised license, and bar re-entry for three years. Students in these programs are the people who have borne the cost when a 'degree' turns out not to qualify them for work.

Online schools must be authorized in every state where their students live, ending the practice of enrolling students in states where the program is not recognized. Compliant providers already meet this; non-compliant ones lose access to out-of-state students.

industries.industry: Traditional colleges and universities with licensure-track programs
industries.note: Legitimate programs would likely already qualify graduates for licensure, but they face new certification paperwork, documentation of prerequisites in every state they advertise to, and responsibility for arranging clinical placements and internships that depend on outside employers.

industries.industry: Recognized accreditors and state licensing agencies
industries.note: Schools must certify programmatic accreditation and licensure prerequisites in each relevant state, giving accreditors and state agencies a larger gatekeeping role over which programs students can fund with federal aid.
